summary:
Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Croatia since 1977, and transgender people may serve openly in the armed forces. Hate-crime legislation enumerates both sexual orientation and gender identity. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 1998 and raised to 15 by the Penal Code that took effect on 1 January 2013.

Enforcement lags the statute book. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records that minority representatives describe anti-discrimination provisions covering employment, housing, education and health as inconsistently enforced, that NGOs report uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases and limited access to justice, and that victims are reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and of being victimised during trial. Hate-crime investigations are flagged as inadequate.

A 2018 Zagreb Pride documentation report on Croatia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 covers hate-crime legislation and under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes, hate-speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, covering 2024, records that a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); that anti-gender disinformation is escalating, with a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' featuring speakers spreading misinformation and no LGBTI organisations invited; and that the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before.

A Croatian legal journal article (Igrec, 2026) analyses how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming persons under Croatian law, working from the 2013 legislative amendment allowing gender-marker registration without altering sex characteristics, through the Criminal Procedure Act, Police Powers Act, Customs Act and prison-sentences law, with case studies of search difficulties. It documents the post-2013 legal framework in practice.

Life partnerships have existed since 2014, following a 2013 constitutional referendum that banned same-sex marriage. Full same-sex adoption rights date from a 2022 final court ruling. Article 68 of the Life Partnership Act grants life partners the same health insurance and healthcare rights as married heterosexual couples and prohibits adverse treatment of life partnerships in those areas. Reproductive care remains unequal: the Medically Supported Fertilization Law limits IVF to married heterosexual couples and single infertile women, effectively excluding same-sex couples; a 2012 law had allowed single women but not lesbian couples. Foster care access for same-sex couples came only through the courts, with the Constitutional Court ruling on 7 February 2020 that exclusion was unconstitutional and discriminatory, and Mladen Kožić and Ivo Šegota becoming Croatia's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year legal battle; as of January 2024 no national law yet regulates same-sex adoption, protections coming only from court rulings. The Center for Social Welfare had initially rejected the Kožić/Šegota application twice.

The blood transfusion institute's rules effectively bar gay and bisexual men from donating blood indefinitely: a 2007 bylaw places men who have sex with men under categories of permanent rejection, and as of 2021 this is framed as 'behaviors or activities that expose them to risk of contracting blood-borne infectious diseases'.

In March 2014 Croatia granted asylum for the first time to a person persecuted on the basis of sexual orientation, a young man from Uganda who fled under the Uganda Anti-homosexuality Act. The sources say nothing about visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry procedures for transgender travellers.

Croatia has three LGBT centres: the first in Zagreb, a second opened in Split on 24 May 2014, and a third in Rijeka on 16 October 2014 (LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka). Zagreb has the biggest gay scene, with clubs, bars and Queer Zagreb programming, while gay-friendly venues and beaches are noted in Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Intrepid Travel's country guide states that Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers but that public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities and that gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik.

In 2009 the European Committee on Social Rights found discriminatory statements in a mandatory Croatian school biology textbook, ruling they violated the European Social Charter; on 1 March 2013 the Minister for Science, Education and Sports announced an action to strip homophobic content from elementary and high school books, especially religious education texts. A Eurobarometer-style survey found 64% of Croatians agreed school lessons should include information about sexual orientation diversity and 63% about gender identity; a 2016 study on children in LGBT families found psychosocial adaptation and experiences of stigmatisation.

In 2023 the opposition Možemo! party proposed easier legal gender change and IVF inclusivity, but none of those bills had passed as of January 2024.

Pride events take place in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula, alongside the Balkans Trans Inter March.
tangentialFactors:
A European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023) assesses transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, placing Croatia under EU monitoring machinery that a visitor cannot invoke directly but that shapes the domestic framework.

The 2018 Zagreb Pride report and the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 both document under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes and escalating anti-gender disinformation, including a parliamentary session on 'Gender Ideology' that featured misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited. Formal protections therefore coexist with documented gaps in reporting and political hostility.

Public visibility carries a mixed picture: the first Pula Pride march in 2024 faced disruption the day before, while the Split LGBT Centre opened in May 2014 ahead of the 4th Split Pride on 7 June 2014, where organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families and mayor Ivo Baldasar attended the press conference. Rijeka's Druga Rijeka centre, presented in October 2014, is backed publicly by mayor Vojko Obersnel and local cultural institutions.
